sections.body:
[Stub: this library does not hold the text of Part III. This section lists what the print holds, from the Guide's Contents, and stores the remaining life equations of p. III-89 with the sentences printed around them. For anything else in Part III, consult the printed Guide.]

Part III, Pavement Design Procedures for Rehabilitation of Existing Pavements, holds five chapters (Contents):

Chapter 1 Introduction (p. III-3): 1.1 Background; 1.2 Scope; 1.3 Assumptions/Limitations; 1.4 Organization.

Chapter 2 Rehabilitation Concepts (p. III-7): 2.1 Background; 2.2 Rehabilitation Factors (2.2.1 Major Categories, 2.2.2 Recycling Concepts, 2.2.3 Construction Considerations, 2.2.4 Summary of Major Rehabilitation Factors); 2.3 Selection of Alternative Rehabilitation Methods (2.3.1 Overview, 2.3.2 Problem Definition, 2.3.3 Potential Problem Solutions, 2.3.4 Selection of Preferred Solution, 2.3.5 Summary).

Chapter 3 Guides for Field Data Collection (p. III-19): 3.1 Overview; 3.2 The Fundamental Analysis Unit (3.2.1 General Background, 3.2.2 Methods of Unit Delineation); 3.3 Drainage Survey for Rehabilitation (3.3.1 Role of Drainage in Rehabilitation, 3.3.2 Assessing Need for Drainage Evaluation, 3.3.3 Pavement History, Topography, and Geometry, 3.3.4 Properties of Materials, 3.3.5 Climatic Zones, 3.3.6 Summary); 3.4 Condition (Distress) Survey (3.4.1 General Background, 3.4.2 Minimum Information Needs, 3.4.3 Utilization of Information); 3.5 NDT Deflection Measurement (3.5.1 Overview, 3.5.2 Uses of NDT Deflection Results, 3.5.3 Evaluating the Effective Structural Capacity, 3.5.4 Joint Load Transfer Analysis, 3.5.5 Use in Slab-Void Detection); 3.6 Field Sampling and Testing Programs (3.6.1 Test Types, 3.6.2 Major Parameters, 3.6.3 Necessity for Destructive Testing, 3.6.4 Selecting the Required Number of Tests).

Chapter 4 Rehabilitation Methods Other Than Overlay (p. III-59): 4.1 Evaluation of Pavement Condition (4.1.1 Surface Distress, 4.1.2 Structural Condition, 4.1.3 Functional Condition); 4.2 Development of Feasible Alternatives and Strategies; 4.3 Major Nonoverlay Methods (4.3.1 Full-Depth Repair, 4.3.2 Partial-Depth Pavement Repair, 4.3.3 Joint and Crack Sealing, 4.3.4 Subsealing of Concrete Pavements, 4.3.5 Diamond Grinding of Concrete Surfaces and Cold Milling of Asphalt Surfaces, 4.3.6 Subdrainage Design, 4.3.7 Pressure Relief Joints, 4.3.8 Restoration of Joint Load Transfer in Jointed Concrete Pavements, 4.3.9 Surface Treatments, 4.3.10 Prediction of Life of Rehabilitation Techniques Without Overlay, p. III-73).

Chapter 5 Rehabilitation Methods With Overlays (p. III-79): 5.1 Overlay Type Feasibility; 5.2 Important Considerations in Overlay Design (5.2.1 Pre-overlay Repair, 5.2.2 Reflection Crack Control, 5.2.3 Traffic Loadings, 5.2.4 Subdrainage, 5.2.5 Rutting in AC Pavements, 5.2.6 Milling AC Surface, 5.2.7 Recycling the Existing Pavement, 5.2.8 Structural versus Functional Overlays, 5.2.9 Overlay Materials, 5.2.10 Shoulders, 5.2.11 Existing PCC Slab Durability, 5.2.12 PCC Overlay Joints, 5.2.13 PCC Overlay Reinforcement, 5.2.14 PCC Overlay Bonding/Separation Layers, 5.2.15 Overlay Design Reliability Level and Overall Standard Deviation, 5.2.16 Pavement Widening, 5.2.17 Potential Errors and Possible Adjustments to Thickness Design Procedure, 5.2.18 Example Designs and Documentation); 5.3 Pavement Evaluation for Overlay Design (5.3.1 Design of Overlay Along Project, 5.3.2 Functional Evaluation of Existing Pavement, 5.3.3 Structural Evaluation of Existing Pavement, p. III-85, 5.3.4 Determination of Design MR, p. III-91). Then one section for each overlay type, each with subsections for feasibility, pre-overlay repair, reflection crack control, subdrainage and thickness design, then shoulders, widening and others: 5.4 AC Overlay of AC Pavement (p. III-94; 5.4.5 Thickness Design, p. III-95); 5.5 AC Overlay of Fractured PCC Slab Pavement (p. III-106; 5.5.5, p. III-108); 5.6 AC Overlay of JPCP, JRCP, and CRCP (p. III-113; 5.6.5, p. III-115); 5.7 AC Overlay of AC/JPCP, AC/JRCP, and AC/CRCP (p. III-125; 5.7.5, p. III-128); 5.8 Bonded Concrete Overlay of JPCP, JRCP, and CRCP (p. III-136; 5.8.5, p. III-137); 5.9 Unbonded JPCP, JRCP, or CRCP Overlay of JPCP, JRCP, CRCP, or AC/PCC (p. III-145; 5.9.5, p. III-146); 5.10 JPCP, JRCP, and CRCP Overlay of AC Pavement (p. III-153; 5.10.5, p. III-154). References for Chapter 5, p. III-157. The Appendices listed in the Contents include M, An Examination of the AASHTO Remaining Life Factor, and N, Overlay Design Examples.

[Note: the Contents list 5.10.8 Reinforcement and then 5.10.10 Widening, with no 5.10.9.]

Remaining life, from Section 5.3.3, Structural Evaluation of Existing Pavement, as printed:

[p. III-89] To determine the remaining life, the designer must determine the actual amount of traffic the pavement has carried to date and the total amount of traffic the pavement could be expected to carry to "failure" (when serviceability equals 1.5, to be consistent with the AASHO Road Test equations). Both traffic amounts must be expressed in 18-kip ESAL. The difference between these values, expressed as a percentage of the total traffic to "failure," is defined as the remaining life:

RL = 100[1 − (Np/N1.5)]

where

RL = remaining life, percent

Np = total traffic to date, 18-kip ESAL

N1.5 = total traffic to pavement "failure" (P2 = 1.5), 18-kip ESAL.

With RL determined, the designer may obtain a condition factor (CF) from Figure 5.2. CF is defined by the equation:

CF = SCn/SCo

where

SCn = pavement structural capacity after Np ESAL

SCo = original pavement structural capacity.

The existing structural capacity may be estimated by multiplying the original structural capacity of the pavement by CF. For example, the original structural number (SNo) of a flexible pavement may be calculated from material thicknesses and the structural coefficients for those materials in a new pavement. SNeff of the pavement based on a remaining life analysis would be:

SNeff = CF * SNo

The structural capacity determined by this relationship does not account for any preoverlay repair. The calculated structural capacity should be viewed as a lower limit value and may require adjustment to reflect the benefits of preoverlay repair.

For the remaining life determination, N1.5 can be roughly estimated using the new pavement design equations or nomographs, or other equations based on local agency information. To be consistent with the AASHO Road Test and the development of these equations, a failure PSI equal to 1.5 and a reliability of 50 percent is recommended.

When using this approach, the designer need not be alarmed if the traffic to date (Np) is found to exceed the expected traffic to failure (N1.5) resulting in a calculated negative remaining life. When this happens, the designer could use the minimum value for CF (0.50), or not use the remaining life approach.

The remaining life approach to determine SNeff or Deff has some serious deficiencies associated with it. There are four major sources of error:

(1) The predictive capability of the AASHO Road Test equations,

(2) The large variation in performance typically observed even among pavements of seemingly identical designs,

(3) Estimation of past 18-kip ESALs, and

(4) Inability to account for the amount of preoverlay repair to the pavement. For pavements with considerable deterioration, the SNeff or Deff value obtained from the remaining life method may be much lower than values obtained from other methods that adjust for preoverlay repairs. Thus, the remaining life procedure is most applicable to pavements which have very little visible deterioration.

[Note: p. III-89 begins inside an earlier paragraph and the text goes on to p. III-90 (two extreme errors of the approach); the rest of Section 5.3.3 and Figure 5.2 are not stored. The decimal points of 1.5 and 0.50 are faint in the scan and are readings.]
